Chapter One: Childhood in Captivity and the Early Realization of Injustice.
Picture this: a world where childhood isn’t defined by laughter and freedom, but by the hard edges of ownership and endless work.
Imagine a little boy, not even sure when his own birthday is. He grows up on a plantation where family bonds are delicate, easily broken at the whim of others.
His earliest memories? They aren’t filled with games or comfort. Instead, they’re marked by loss—being separated from his mother, who’s only allowed to see him at night. Her visits are brief, and every bit of affection comes in tiny doses, rationed out by the demands of her labor.
And as for a father? Well, in this world, not having one around isn’t strange at all. If you ask about paternity, all you get are rumors or silence.
Here, children aren’t brought up by their parents, but by older women—caretakers who look after the young while the adults work the fields.
Days pass with empty bellies and the barest meals; nights are spent sleeping on cold floors, wrapped in nothing but a rough cloth for warmth.
The sense of belonging is fragile, and most kids only know their family through whispered stories or the briefest, stolen moments together.
As this child grows, the true nature of slavery slowly comes into focus. There’s always this sense of being watched—every move, every word, judged by those in charge. The plantation has its own rules, its own hierarchy, and everyone learns early on to hide what they really feel.
Even laughter and singing are measured, because too much joy? That could be seen as a threat.
The first real lessons in injustice don’t come from any book. They come from what the child sees every day. Some people get special treatment, while others are punished for the tiniest mistake.
There’s this deep sense that things just aren’t fair, but hardly anyone says it out loud. Most folks have learned to accept it, believing there’s no point in fighting back.
And yet, even here, you’ll find moments of quiet rebellion—a stolen moment of rest, a whispered word of hope, a longing for something better.
The plantation is full of contradictions. The enslavers talk about religion and morality, but their actions? They tell a different story.
The child notices how sometimes kindness is just another way to control, and cruelty is always explained away as “necessary” for order and discipline. The hypocrisy isn’t lost, even on the youngest.
Over time, the child is sent to live with new people, each move bringing fresh challenges and unfamiliar faces. There’s this constant feeling of instability, and the fear of being separated from what little family remains never really goes away.
Through it all, there’s a growing sense that life could be different, that maybe there’s something beyond the plantation—possibilities no one here dares to imagine.
These early years are all about a slow awakening. The child starts to see that slavery isn’t just the way things are—it’s something forced on them, held in place by fear and violence.
And even though the seeds of resistance are hidden for now, you can feel them quietly taking root, just waiting for their chance to grow.
